namespace LO.IntProp.Formula

variable {α : Type u} {ℍ : Type*} [HeytingAlgebra ℍ] (v : α → ℍ)
informal_statement: For any formula \( \varphi \) in a given vocabulary \( \alpha \), the truth value of its negation under any valuation \( v \) is the complement of its original truth value under the same valuation. In mathematical notation, \( \text{∼φ}.\text{hVal}(v) = (\varphi.\text{hVal}(v))^\complement \).
informal_proof:
This statement is a fundamental property of how negation interacts with truth values. To prove it, we rely directly on the definitions of negation and the `hVal` function. Specifically, the `∼` operator in Lean represents the negation of a proposition, and the `hVal` function returns the truth value of a formula under a given valuation. The right-hand side, `(\varphi.\text{hVal}(v))^\complement`, denotes the complement of the set containing the truth value of \( \varphi \) under \( v \).

Given that `∼φ` is the negation of \( \varphi \), and the truth value of a negation is the complement of the original truth value, the equality \( \varphi.\text{hVal}(v) = (\text{∼φ}).\text{hVal}(v)^\complement \) holds by definition. Therefore, the proof follows directly from the definitions involved, and the `rfl` tactic is sufficient to confirm this equality as a tautology.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
